notes: Complete EWCA Civ judgment dismissing appeal against Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal strike-off.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor's strike-off upheld after in absentia SDT hearing and catalogue of professional misconduct
key_facts: Mr Awan was struck off the Roll by the Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal in his absence on 7 August 2001 after ten proved charges of conduct unbefitting a solicitor.

The charges concerned failure to pay transcribers', expert witness and counsel fees, breach of undertakings, obstruction of Law Society account inspections, and failure to deliver accountant's reports.

He appealed via the Administrative Court (dismissed December 2001) and then to the Court of Appeal; the SDT had refused an adjournment because he produced only an inadequate social security medical certificate rather than the required doctor's report and prognosis.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of appeal from the Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal strike-off decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; SDT strike-off upheld with costs; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A disciplinary tribunal may proceed in a solicitor's absence where he fails on the balance of probabilities to establish genuine inability to attend; regulatory conditions on a practising certificate are protective not punitive and do not preclude SDT sanction; a pattern of evasion and prevariation over years can justify strike-off without a specific charge of dishonesty.
legal_issues: Whether the SDT acted unfairly in refusing an adjournment and proceeding in Mr Awan's absence
Whether denial of legal aid before the SDT breached Article 6
Whether OSS practising certificate conditions amounted to double punishment
Whether strike-off was disproportionate and required proof of dishonesty

enrichment.short_title: Football club's £29m bank demand claim struck out after ineffective contractual demand
key_facts: Bournemouth & Boscombe Athletic Football Club claimed almost £29 million damages after Lloyds TSB demanded immediate repayment under a 1994 refinancing agreement on 2 July 1996.
The Club contended the demand was wrongful because Gardiner's £250,000 cash deposit should have been treated as satisfying the Club's payment obligation.

Particulars of Claim were served 11 days late in a second action after an earlier action had been struck out for the same procedural failure; Peter Smith J refused an extension and struck out the claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against strike-out and refusal to extend time for service of Particulars of Claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; claim struck out as bound to fail; costs of £40,000 ordered against the Club.
enrichment.ratio: A contractual demand made without entitlement and devoid of legal significance is not a breach of contract; even if wrongful, an ineffective demand cannot found a claim for loss where the bank had no obligation to continue financial support beyond the facility terms.
legal_issues: Whether failure to serve particulars in time was deliberate for CPR 3.9 purposes
Whether the Club had a viable claim that the 2 July 1996 demand breached the 1994 Agreement
Whether the Bank could rely on insolvency as an Event of Default when demand was based on payment default
Whether the second action was an abuse of process

enrichment.short_title: HSE decision not to prosecute over fatal falling door upheld as reasonably open

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work etc Act 1974
Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999

key_facts: Christopher Pullen, aged 12, died on 13 September 2000 after a heavy communal security door fell on him at Southdown House on Islington's Market Estate.
Islington owned the estate; Hyde Housing Association held the maintenance contract from July 2000; the door had been off its hinges since at least 19 June 2000.
Mrs Pullen sought judicial review of the HSE's decision not to prosecute Islington or Hyde; the HSE concluded there was no realistic prospect of conviction under the CPS two-stage test.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of the Health and Safety Executive's decision not to institute criminal proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review dismissed; HSE non-prosecution decision held reasonably open.
enrichment.ratio: A decision not to prosecute is reviewable only on narrow grounds including unlawful policy, failure to follow the Code for Crown Prosecutors, or perversity; where proposed defendants had reasonably practicable maintenance systems and evidence did not sufficiently establish employee default or the duration of the hazard, a prosecutor could reasonably conclude the evidential test was not met.
legal_issues: Grounds for judicial review of prosecutorial discretion
Elements of section 3(1) HSWA offence and reverse burden under section 40
Whether witness perceptions of danger were relevant to prosecutorial assessment
Whether injury alone established exposure to risk under R v Associated Octel

notes: Complete Divisional Court judgment on youth court mode of trial and committal following dropped robbery charge.

enrichment.short_title: Youth Court must revert to summary trial when serious robbery charge dropped leaving adequate sentencing powers
key_facts: A 15-year-old (H) was charged with two street robberies including theft of a mobile phone from a schoolboy and a violent home robbery with racial abuse.
Balham Youth Court declined summary jurisdiction in March 2003 when both charges remained, then committed H for trial after the more serious charge was dropped in April 2003.
Neither defence nor prosecution addressed section 25(7) MCA 1980 at the committal hearing to revert to summary trial once only the lesser robbery remained.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of Balham Youth Court decisions declining summary jurisdiction and committing for Crown Court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge to March decision dismissed; April committal decision quashed; mandatory order that Youth Court try the case summarily.
enrichment.ratio: Where a youth aged 15–17 faces section 91 offences, the Youth Court should commit only if a custodial sentence exceeding 24 months is a real possibility; once the more serious charge is abandoned leaving only a single mobile-phone robbery, section 25(7) requires the court during committal inquiry to switch to summary trial because Youth Court sentencing powers are adequate.
legal_issues: When a real possibility of section 91 detention longer than two years exists
Power under section 25(7) to revert from committal to summary trial mid-hearing
Appropriate sentence bracket for 15-year-old mobile phone robbery

notes: Complete EWCA Crim judgment on directed conviction and section 139 blade possession defences.

enrichment.short_title: Directed conviction upheld where Shaolin martial arts defence could not satisfy section 139 good or religious reason
key_facts: Chinese asylum seeker Wang was found at Clacton Railway Station holding a sheathed curved sword and carrying a kukri-style knife in his bag while detaining a suspected thief.
He claimed Shaolin Buddhist practice required carrying weapons and constituted good reason or religious reason under section 139(4) and (5)(b).

The trial judge directed the jury to convict on both counts after finding the defence incapable in law; Wang had told police he was travelling to see his immigration solicitor and took the weapons because nowhere safe to leave them.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by direction following trial at Chelmsford Crown Court.
enrichment.ratio: Where the defendant bears the evidential burden on a section 139 defence, a judge may direct conviction if the account is incapable as a matter of law of showing good reason or religious reason; martial arts practice must be the predominant motivation for possession on the specific occasion, and convenience because no one was at home to safeguard weapons is not a good reason.
legal_issues: Limits on judicial power to direct jury conviction where defendant carries evidential burden
Scope of 'good reason' and 'religious reasons' under section 139(4) and (5)(b)
Whether Article 9 ECHR requires additional protection beyond the statutory defences

enrichment.short_title: US tobacco RICO letters of request granted for solicitor Foyle but refused for chairman Broughton as impermissible fishing

statutes_considered.title: Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act 1970 (US)

key_facts: The United States sought examination of Lovells partner Andrew Foyle and BAT plc chairman Martin Broughton for evidence in a $289 billion RICO action against tobacco companies in Washington D.C.
Foyle had advised BAT group companies from 1985–1994 on document management, smoking-and-health litigation and disclosure; the US alleged systematic document destruction and privilege abuse.
BATCo intervened claiming blanket legal advice and litigation privilege; the US offered Foyle immunity and undertook not to pursue civil proceedings against him.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications under the 1975 Act to give effect to letters of request from the US District Court for the District of Columbia.
enrichment.outcome: Order for Foyle's examination before a High Court judge granted with directions; application relating to Broughton refused as impermissibly investigatory.
enrichment.ratio: Privilege under section 3(1)(a) of the 1975 Act may justify refusing examination only in the clearest blanket-privilege cases; following Three Rivers, legal advice privilege requires dominant purpose of obtaining rights-and-obligations advice and litigation privilege requires litigation reasonably in prospect; a letter of request must not be acceded to where its main purpose is impermissible oral discovery rather than trial evidence.
legal_issues: Scope of legal advice privilege after Three Rivers District Council v Bank of England (No 5)
When litigation privilege attaches to document review preparations
Whether waiver occurred through Minnesota settlement and public document release
Whether letters of request amounted to impermissible fishing or investigatory examination

enrichment.short_title: Claim for return of seized cash struck out after eight years' inaction and unanswered disclosure requests
key_facts: Irish resident Fay left over £390,000 cash in luggage at Luton Airport in July 1993; Bedfordshire Police seized it and arrested him for suspected money laundering.

No prosecution followed but the Chief Constable refused return; Fay issued proceedings in May 1994 then took no steps for eight years after failing to answer further particulars requests in September 1994.
In 2002 the Chief Constable applied to lift the CPR automatic stay, strike out for want of prosecution, and dispose of the cash under Police (Property) Regulations 1997.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against first-instance decision lifting automatic stay and allowing claim to continue.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claim struck out; Chief Constable permitted to dispose of funds under regulation 6(4).
enrichment.ratio: An eight-year delay with only a flimsy excuse, failure to answer legitimate enquiries about the origin of seized cash, and impossibility of fair investigation after nine years justify strike-out; the Chief Constable could not enquire into better title until the claimant answered questions he still refused to address.

Whether delay amounted to abuse of process or abandonment under Grovit v Doctor principles
Whether a fair trial remained possible on title to seized cash

enrichment.short_title: Privacy claimant need not disclose full post-publication witness statements where truth is not pleaded issue
key_facts: Senior police officer Brian Paddick claimed damages and injunction for breach of privacy/confidence over Mail on Sunday articles about his personal relationships and private life published in March 2002.
The defendant relied on public interest and ostensibly credible sourcing from James Renolleau and Fiona Chambers without pleading truth of the allegations.
Paddick disclosed extracts only from post-publication witness statements; the defendant sought full statements and an order that it provide transcripts of disclosed interview tapes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications in defamation/privacy proceedings for further disclosure and costs of transcript application.
enrichment.outcome: Application for full witness statements refused; defendant ordered to provide transcripts by 31 December 2003; claimant's costs of transcript application in the case.
enrichment.ratio: Truth or falsity of allegations is not part of a party's case for standard disclosure where the defence rests on ostensibly credible information and public interest, not pleaded truth; a party may withhold irrelevant portions of documents on oath of irrelevance under GE Capital principles; post-publication materials do not relate to pleaded issues in such a defence.
legal_issues: Whether truth/falsity became a disclosure issue because the claimant's witness statement denied allegations
Relevance of post-publication witness statements to public interest balancing
Whether disclosing party must provide intelligible transcripts of disclosed audio tapes
Application of Reynolds/Spycatcher ostensibly credible allegation standard to privacy claims

enrichment.short_title: Ear-print burglary convictions safe despite Dallagher fresh evidence where defendant admitted print and lied
key_facts: Kempster was convicted of four burglaries targeting elderly victims in Hampshire in June 2000, including one where his ear-print was found on a forced kitchen window at 89-year-old Mrs Hooker's home.

Expert Cheryl McGowan matched the scene print to Kempster's ear; he accepted the print was his but claimed innocent explanations and gave a detailed alibi after initially denying visiting the premises.
Mid-trial he dismissed counsel seeking fresh representation; the Recorder refused adjournment and Kempster continued unrepresented, with his wife eventually reading much of his closing speech.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and sentence to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) with fresh expert evidence under section 23 CAA 1968.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals against conviction and sentence dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh evidence from Professor Champod following R v Dallagher would not have affected the jury where the defendant admitted the ear-print, lied repeatedly about his presence and alibi, and had substantial supporting circumstantial evidence; a judge properly exercised discretion in refusing fresh counsel where dismissal appeared a device to secure retrial after failed no-case submission.
legal_issues: Admissibility and weight of ear-print identification evidence after Dallagher
Whether fresh expert evidence under section 23 rendered convictions unsafe
Fairness of continuing trial without fresh counsel under Article 6
Propriety of allowing alibi witness to read defendant's closing speech
